# `invalidated-element-pointer`

<!-- rule-docs:header (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
Tier: correctness · Profile: none · Default: warning · Fixes: none · Options: none

Reports a pointer into a sequence or hash-map entry used after an operation that
may reallocate or rehash the backing storage.
<!-- /rule-docs:header -->

## Why it matters

Container growth can move its allocation and invalidate element pointers even
though the container itself remains valid.

## When it fires

It applies to pointers derived from `.items` storage or from `addOne` and
`addManyAs*`, and to entry-returning methods such as `getEntry`, `getPtr`, and
`getOrPut`, followed by an invalidating mutation of the same container: growth,
a rehash, or a removal (`remove` only of the same key, `swapRemove` and
`orderedRemove` of any). The container is recognized by its declared type, so
`var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty` and `= try .initCapacity(gpa, n)` count
like the older `std.ArrayList(u8).empty`; it may also be a field or a function
parameter. Visible aliases and summarized helper mutations preserve the
container identity.

A later use counts only when control flow can reach it: a mutation in a branch
that returns does not taint the sibling branch, comparing only the pointer
value is not a use, `orderedRemove(k)` leaves a pointer to a literal element
index below `k` valid, and `ensureUnusedCapacity` followed by `...AssumeCapacity`
calls stays quiet.

<!-- rule-docs:footer (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
## Example

```zig
const std = @import("std");

fn run(allocator: std.mem.Allocator) !void {
    var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(allocator);
    try list.append(allocator, 1);
    const first = &list.items[0];
    try list.append(allocator, 2);
    first.* = 3;
}
```
